title: The “I'm Fine” Mask
hook: “I'm fine” is the sentence men use most to close a door, and the body standing behind it often says the door should be knocked on, gently.
why:
*I'm fine* is the most useful sentence in social life. It ends small talk, spares other people, keeps work moving and is usually true. But it is also the sentence that most often stands between a man who is struggling and the people who could help him. It is said by men going through divorces, redundancies, bereavements and long periods of low mood, often with a smile, often to people who would have helped if they had known.

This chapter is about reading past the sentence without disrespecting it. You will learn why so many men keep the mask on, what holding feelings in costs both the person and the people around him, what the mask tends to look like from outside, and how to ask in a way that makes it easier to answer honestly: twice, side by side, and with real listening. It ends with when *fine* is not enough, and what to do then. Nothing here is a way of diagnosing anyone. It is a way of noticing, and of being someone people can tell.

teach.h: Fine is a door, not always a statement.
teach.p:
Most of the time, *I'm fine* means exactly that, or near enough. It is also the expected answer to *How are you?*, a ritual exchange rather than a real question, and treating every *fine* as a confession waiting to happen would be exhausting and intrusive.

But the sentence also does another job. It closes a door that the person is not ready to open, or does not believe anyone wants opened. In surveys carried out in England for a public campaign called Ask Twice, most respondents said they would tell people they were fine even if they were struggling with a mental health problem. Many said they did not want to be a burden, or did not think the person asking really wanted to know.

So the question for a reader is not whether *fine* is true in general, but whether it fits everything else this person is showing you. The tools of the earlier chapters apply directly. What is this person's baseline? Has anything changed, in their voice, their posture, their habits, their sleep, their drinking, their humour? Do the channels agree, as the chapter on clusters and congruence asked, or does a cheerful word sit on top of a flat voice and a body that has stopped moving?

When *fine* arrives with everything else at baseline, take it at face value. When it arrives with a cluster of changes, it may be a door worth knocking on, gently.

The word is only one channel. Read it with the others.
teach.disconfirm: If people who said they were fine while showing several changes from their baseline turned out, when you got to know more, to be just as fine as anyone else, reading past the word would add nothing. Most people can think of at least one *fine* that was not.

teach.p:
In 2003 Michael Addis and James Mahalik reviewed the research on why men seek help less often than women for physical and mental health problems. They argued that the gap is not simply about men being stubborn. It depends on context. Men tend to seek help less when the problem feels unusual, as if no other man has it; when asking for help means giving up control; when the problem touches something central to their sense of themselves; and when the people around them would see help-seeking as weakness. When those conditions change, men's help-seeking changes too.

Research for the Ask Twice campaign found that many men said they would not open up to friends about their mental health for fear of being seen as a burden. The fear was not of the feeling itself but of what saying it would cost: being pitied, being a nuisance, being seen differently, losing a place in a group that runs on banter.

This matters for a reader because it explains what makes the mask easier to lower. It is easier when the problem is shown to be ordinary, *loads of people go through this*; when the person keeps control of what happens next; when asking for help can be framed as practical rather than as weakness; and when the person asking clearly wants to know.

It also explains why the mask is not a lie in any ordinary sense. It is usually an attempt to protect other people, a relationship, or a sense of self, and many men believe it themselves until something makes it impossible.
teach.disconfirm: If men sought help just as readily whatever the context, whether problems seemed common or rare and whether help meant losing control, the account in this block would be wrong. The research reviewed by Addis and Mahalik found context mattered a great deal.

teach.h: Holding it in costs both people.
teach.p:
Keeping a feeling off the face and out of the voice is effortful. In 2003 James Gross and Oliver John studied people who habitually suppress the expression of their emotions, compared with people who more often reappraise situations, changing how they think about them. Habitual suppressors reported more negative emotion, lower wellbeing and fewer close relationships, and their friends described them as less close and less socially supported.

The cost spreads. In 2003 Emily Butler and colleagues paired strangers to discuss an upsetting topic, and asked one person in some pairs to hide their emotional reactions. The conversations went less well: communication was disrupted, rapport was lower, and the partners of the people suppressing had higher blood pressure than partners in other conversations. The other person could not see what was being hidden, but they felt that something was.

This is why the mask is so often noticed even when it is not seen through. Family, friends and colleagues sense that a man is somewhere else, that conversations have become oddly effortful, that his warmth has thinned. They may not connect it with anything, and may simply feel that he has become harder to be around.

For a reader, that sense of effort is itself a clue. When conversations with someone you know well have started to feel like work, and you cannot say why, the work may be the mask.

A mask is felt by everyone near it, even when nobody can see what is behind it.
teach.disconfirm: If people suppressing their feelings had no effect on how their conversation partners felt or responded, the mask would cost only the wearer. The studies described here found effects on partners too.

teach.h: What the mask looks like from outside.
teach.p:
The mask rarely looks like sadness. More often it looks like something else: constant jokes, sometimes with a harder edge than usual; being very busy, at work late, always doing something; irritability, a short fuse with partners and children; drinking more, or more often alone; risk-taking, driving fast, gambling; withdrawal from things he used to enjoy, the regular game, the pub with friends, the hobby.

In 2013 Lisa Martin, Harold Neighbors and Derek Griffith analysed a large American survey and found that when measures of depression included symptoms such as anger attacks, aggression, substance use and risk-taking alongside the more familiar symptoms, men and women met the criteria at similar rates. The usual gap, in which women appear far more often depressed, largely disappeared. The researchers suggested that the conventional symptom lists may miss many men whose distress shows in other ways.

The body joins in. The smile is there, but the chapter on clusters would note that it comes without the rest: the voice may be flat, the eyes may not lift, the posture may sag the moment the person thinks nobody is looking. Sleep changes, appetite changes and the slow drift of a baseline, described in the chapter on the stress posture, are often visible to the people who see him every day.

None of these is a diagnosis, and each has many ordinary causes. A man who is busy may simply be busy. What makes them worth noticing is a change from the person's own baseline, several at once, lasting weeks.
teach.disconfirm: If changes such as more drinking, irritability, withdrawal and constant joking were no more common in men who were struggling than in men who were not, they would tell you nothing. The survey research described here suggests they are part of how distress shows in many men.

teach.p:
The idea behind the Ask Twice campaign is simple. The first *How are you?* gets the ritual answer. A second question, asked with evident interest, tells the person that you really want to know, and gives them a chance to say more.

The second question works best when it is specific and about something you have noticed, described as behaviour, not as a verdict. *You've not been at five-a-side for a few weeks. Everything all right?* is easier to answer than *You seem depressed*. It works best in private, and when there is time to answer. And it works best with an exit, so that the person keeps control: *No pressure. Just checking.*

Then the hard part: wait. Many men need a moment, or several, before they say anything real. A silence after your question is not a refusal. It is often the sound of someone deciding whether to trust you. If you fill it, you close the door they were about to open.

Sometimes the answer will still be *I'm fine*, and sometimes that will be true. Accept it, without pressing, and leave the door open: *All right. If that changes, I'm around.* Many men come back days or weeks later to a person who asked twice and did not push.

Timing matters as much as wording. Avoid asking in passing as someone heads into a meeting, or late at night after drinks, when an honest answer has nowhere safe to go. If you cannot be with the person, a message can do part of the work: *Been thinking about you. Fancy a walk at the weekend?* It asks nothing yet, and it creates the side-by-side moment in which the real question can come.

The second question is often the first real one.
teach.disconfirm: If asking a second time, specifically and privately, produced no more honest answers than asking once, the second question would not be worth the awkwardness. Try it with someone who has seemed different lately, and notice what happens.
teach.pullQuote: The second question is often the first real one.

teach.h: Side by side, and listen rather than fix.
teach.p:
Many men find it easier to talk when they do not have to look at the person they are talking to. In the car, on a walk, fishing, fixing something, watching a match: shoulder to shoulder, with something else to look at, the pressure of eye contact drops, as the chapters on proxemics and the gaze described. Part III develops this as the side-by-side principle. If you want to ask twice, choose a moment like this.

When someone does start to talk, the next danger is fixing. Most people respond to another person's difficulty by offering solutions, silver linings or comparisons: *Have you tried...?*, *At least you've still got...*, *When that happened to me...*. Each is well meant, and each tends to end the conversation, because it signals that you want the problem settled more than you want to hear it.

Listening is different. Ask open questions: *What's that been like?* Reflect what you heard: *Sounds like it's been building for a while.* Let silences sit. Resist the urge to make it better before you understand it. Part VI described research showing that people who were listened to well became less anxious and more able to understand their own thoughts. Being listened to is often the help.

Practical help can come later, when it has been asked for or when the person has said enough for you to know what would actually be useful.

The best thing to say is often the thing that lets them say more.
teach.disconfirm: If men talked just as easily face to face across a table as side by side, and if offering solutions early helped as much as listening, this block would be wrong. Notice which conversations in your own life have gone deepest, and where you were sitting.

teach.p:
Most masks hide ordinary hard times that pass with a little support. Some hide more. The signs that a person may need more than a friend's ear are mostly about duration and depth: changes lasting several weeks; sleep that is badly disrupted night after night; withdrawal from almost everything he used to care about; drinking that has become a way of getting through each day; talk of hopelessness, of being a burden, of not seeing the point.

When you see these, encourage him to see a doctor, and make it practical. Offer to help find the number, to go with him, to drive him there. Frame it as ordinary: doctors see this every day, and treatments for low mood and anxiety work for many people. Respect his control over what happens, but do not let the subject drop.

If anything he says or does makes you worried for his safety, the chapter on suicidal ideation later in this part explains what to do, and the most important point is this: ask him directly whether he is thinking about suicide. Asking does not put the idea in his head; reviews of the research have found it does not increase suicidal thinking. The crisis resources in this app are one tap from the home screen, for him and for you.

And look after yourself. Supporting someone through a hard time is demanding, and you are allowed to have limits, to ask others to help, and to talk to someone yourself.
teach.disconfirm: If people whose struggles lasted weeks and disrupted sleep and daily life recovered as readily with a friend's support alone as with professional help, encouraging a doctor's appointment would add little. For most such difficulties, the evidence is that treatment helps.

poseGallery.doCaption: Noticing the changes, and finding a side-by-side moment.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Taking the joke and the 'I'm fine' at face value, again.
poseGallery.annotation: The mask often looks like humour, busyness or irritability. A change from baseline, lasting weeks, is worth a second question.

poseGallery.doCaption: 'You've not been at five-a-side for a while. All right?'
poseGallery.annotation: A verdict invites denial. A specific, behaviour-first question with an exit is easier to answer honestly.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting the silence sit, and asking what it's been like.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Jumping in with solutions as soon as he starts talking.
poseGallery.annotation: Fixing tends to end the conversation. Being listened to is often the help.

poseGallery.doCaption: Accepting it, and leaving the door open.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Moving on when he says 'fine' a second time.
poseGallery.annotation: Pressing harder rarely works. Many men come back later to the person who asked twice and did not push.

caseStudy:
Mike, forty-five, has played five-a-side every Thursday for years with his friend Danny. In the spring Danny's wife moves out. Danny tells everyone he is fine, makes a few jokes about having the remote to himself, and carries on.

Over the next two months, Mike notices changes. Danny misses three Thursdays, then four. When he does come, he goes to the pub afterwards and stays after everyone else has left. His jokes have an edge they did not have before. On the phone his voice is flat and slow, nothing like the Danny who used to talk over everyone. When Mike asks how he is, he says *fine, mate, all good*, and changes the subject.

Mike thinks about how to ask. He does not want to make it a big conversation across a table. He asks Danny to help him collect a sofa from his sister's, an hour's drive each way. On the way back, both of them looking at the road, Mike says: *You've not been at five-a-side much. Are you all right? Really?* Danny says *yeah, fine*. Mike says nothing. A mile later, Danny says he is not sleeping, that the house is too quiet, that he has been drinking most nights to get to sleep, and that he feels like he has made a mess of everything.

Mike does not try to fix it. He asks what it has been like, and listens for the rest of the drive. Before they get back, he says he thinks Danny should talk to his doctor about the sleep and the drinking, and offers to sit with him while he rings for an appointment. Danny says he will think about it. Two days later he texts: *booked it.*

Danny comes to five-a-side the following Thursday. He is quiet, and he stays for one drink, not five.
observe: Notice the next three times someone tells you they are fine, and whether everything else about them agrees with the word.
Think of one person you know well, and note anything about their habits, humour or voice that has changed over the past few months.
Notice where you are sitting the next time a conversation goes deeper than usual: across a table, at an angle, or side by side.

drills.name: Fine Check
steps: For a week, notice each time someone tells you they are fine.
For each, note whether their voice, posture and recent habits fit the word.
Mark any case where several things did not fit.
For those, write one specific, behaviour-first question you could ask.
Ask it, privately and with an exit, in one case where it feels right.

drills.name: Second Question
steps: Choose someone who has seemed different lately.
Write down the specific change you have noticed, as behaviour, not as a verdict.
Choose a side-by-side moment, such as a drive, a walk or a shared task.
Ask once in the usual way, then ask a second time about the change, and wait through any silence.
Afterwards, write what happened and what you would do differently.

drills.name: Listening, Not Fixing
steps: With a willing friend, ask them to tell you about something mildly frustrating in their week.
For five minutes, use only open questions, reflections and silence; offer no advice or comparisons.
Notice each time you feel the urge to fix or compare, and let it pass.
Ask your friend afterwards how it felt to be listened to that way.
Swap roles, and note what it was like to be on the other side.

drills.name: Your Own Mask
steps: Think of a time when you told people you were fine when you were not.
Write down what you were protecting by saying it: other people, a relationship, an image of yourself.
Write down what, if anything, would have made it easier to say more.
Note who, if anyone, noticed, and how.
Write the name of one person you could tell next time.

drills.name: Know the Next Step
steps: Find out how to book an appointment with a doctor where you live, and note it.
Find the crisis resources in this app and note the number for your region.
Write down two practical offers you could make to someone who needs a doctor, such as finding the number or going with them.
Write down one sentence that frames seeing a doctor as ordinary.
Keep these notes where you can find them quickly.

quiz.q: A friend tells you he is fine. What does this chapter suggest you do?
options: Take it as the final word, since pressing him would be an intrusion
Assume he is hiding something, and press him until he tells you
If other things about him have changed, ask again, gently and specifically
Tell him plainly that you can see he is not fine, so he can stop pretending
quiz.explain: Usually fine is true or close enough. When it comes with a cluster of changes from his baseline, a second, specific question asked privately and with an exit gives him a real chance to say more, without being pressed or labelled.

quiz.q: In Butler and colleagues' study, what happened when one person hid their emotional reactions during a conversation?
options: The partner's blood pressure rose and the conversation flowed less well
The partner noticed nothing at all and the conversation went normally
The partner became more relaxed, since there was less emotion to manage
The partner immediately guessed the exact feeling that was being hidden
quiz.explain: Suppression disrupted communication and reduced rapport, and partners of suppressors showed higher blood pressure. A mask is felt by the people near it even when they cannot see what is behind it.

quiz.q: What did Martin, Neighbors and Griffith find when depression measures included anger attacks, substance use and risk-taking?
options: Men turned out to be far more often depressed than women were
Women's rates of depression rose and men's stayed exactly the same
The new symptoms turned out to be unrelated to depression in anyone
Men and women met the criteria for depression at similar rates
quiz.explain: Conventional symptom lists may miss many men whose distress shows as anger, drinking or risk-taking. When those were included, the usual gap largely disappeared, though none of these signs is a diagnosis on its own.

quiz.q: Your brother says he is fine, but he has stopped coming to family meals, is drinking more, and his jokes have a harder edge. What fits this chapter?
options: Tell the rest of the family that he is depressed so they can help
Find a side-by-side moment and ask again, about the changes you have seen
Leave it, since he has told you he is fine and adults can manage themselves
Tell him directly that he has a drinking problem and needs to stop now
quiz.explain: Several changes from his baseline, lasting weeks, are worth a second question. Side by side and specific about what you have seen, without labels, it is easier for him to answer honestly.

quiz.q: What did Gross and John find about people who habitually suppress the expression of their emotions?
options: They had higher wellbeing, since they were rarely troubled by emotion
They were rated by friends as especially close and well supported
They had lower wellbeing and fewer close relationships than reappraisers
They showed no differences at all from people who reappraise situations
quiz.explain: Habitual suppression went with more negative emotion, lower wellbeing and less close support. Holding feelings in is costly, which is part of why the mask matters.

quiz.q: You ask a colleague a second time how he is, and he says he would rather not talk about it. What fits this chapter?
options: Accept it and leave the door open: 'If that changes, I'm around.'
Keep asking every day until he finally agrees to talk about it
Tell his manager, so that someone with authority can step in now
Point out the signs you have noticed so that he cannot deny them
quiz.explain: He keeps control, which makes it easier to come back later. Many men return to the person who asked twice without pushing. If you are worried about his safety, though, ask directly, as the chapter on suicidal ideation explains.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific time when someone told you they were fine and you later learned they were not, or when you said it yourself. What did the body, the voice and the habits show at the time? Who noticed, and what did they do? If you could go back, how and where would you have asked a second time, and what would you have said, word for word? Then name one person you could ask twice in the coming week.
reflection.guidance: Many men find their example in their own life rather than someone else's, and that is just as useful. Try to describe the changes as behaviour, before any interpretation. The word-for-word question matters: writing it down makes it far easier to say when the moment comes. The last part is the point of the chapter, so choose a real person.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to accept every *fine* at face value, even when everything else about a person has changed for weeks. The opposite failure is to treat every *fine* as a lie, pressing people until they feel inspected and close the door harder. A third is to ask in the wrong way: across a table, in front of others, with a label such as *depressed* that invites denial. A fourth is to fix too fast, offering solutions and silver linings before you have listened, which ends the conversation. And the most serious is to stop at a friend's ear when someone needs more: encourage a doctor, make it practical, and if you are worried about safety, ask directly and use the crisis resources.
